## The Museum of Almost-Remembered Things

The museum occupied a narrow building between a locksmith’s shop and a bakery that opened before sunrise. Its door was painted the particular green of old diving helmets, and above the handle hung a small brass sign:

**THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST-REMEMBERED THINGS**  
**Open whenever you are ready to remember something.**

There was no entrance fee, but the guard at the desk asked each visitor one question:

“What sound do you remember almost hearing?”

I went there on a rainy Tuesday, partly because I had nothing better to do and partly because I was tired of forgetting things.

The first exhibit was a bicycle bell mounted inside a glass case. A card explained that the owner could no longer remember the street where she had ridden it, the name of the boy who raced her downhill, or whether the bell had ever frightened a dog. Still, whenever she pressed it, her hand remembered exactly how hard to press.

In another room came the dry whisper of a subway ticket being validated. A man stood before the exhibit with his eyes closed, shoulders moving as though the invisible turnstile were before him.

There was the click of a light switch in an empty hallway.

The scrape of a chair across a dance floor.

A grandmother’s alarm clock sounding through two closed doors.

Rain beginning on a metal roof.

Someone humming three notes of a song, then becoming uncertain.

And there were smells, too: dust warmed by a cinema projector, toast burning in a hotel room, chalk mixed with rain. Each was kept in a sealed room with a small fan, though the fan did nothing except make the waiting more official.

The curator was a tall woman named Veda, who wore gray gloves and spoke in a voice as soft as a page turning.

“We do not collect memories,” she told me. “Memories are too large, and they change whenever we look at them. We collect the shapes they leave behind.”

At the end of our tour, she led me into an empty room.

“What will you leave with you?” she asked.

I listened.

From somewhere behind the walls came the muffled rhythm of pipes. In the bakery next door, a tray was set down with a metallic clang. Rain tapped the windows, and somewhere outside, a car engine turned over, coughed, and drove away.

The room filled with all the small sounds of the world continuing without me.

Then Veda raised one finger.

Beneath everything, I heard it: my own footsteps, fading down a corridor I could not see.

I realized, with a little panic, that this was the direction in which I would have to leave.

Veda smiled and unlocked the green door.
